Each seed controls a separate graph, initial state and Poisson stream; reuse that seed's graph/initial state and random-number keys across conditions for matched comparisons. Display seed 101 and the final 500 ms, with one sample of 50 unique neurons drawn uniformly from all 12500 using seed 20261108 and fixed across runs.
- Each run lasts 4000 ms; exclude first 1000 ms from every scientific summary. This removes 50 membrane time constants and leaves 3 s for 0.333-Hz Fourier spacing. Finite-window limitations remain explicit. No equilibration-dependent extensions or selected favorable seeds.
- Voltage reference: zero leak equilibrium; between jumps dV/dt=-V/tau_m. With no supplied resting potential, choose the zero defining the supplied threshold/reset voltage differences. No lower voltage clamp, noise current, adaptation or synaptic filtering.
- Graph: uniform fixed indegree, without replacement within each source population; exclude autapses; no parallel recurrent edges. Independent choices for different targets. E and I projections share a common 1.5-ms delay. Connectivity stays fixed during each run. External afferents are independent across targets and recurrent activity, so exactly superpose their Poisson processes into one Poisson count per target per step.
- Initial condition: independent uniform V in [10,20) mV, no refractory neurons, empty recurrent delay history. This spreads phases without presupposing synchrony.
- Integration: dt=0.1 ms, exact exponential leak between grid endpoints, instantaneous recurrent and external jumps at endpoints, then threshold detection and reset. Spikes emitted at t arrive at t+1.5 ms. During refractory, hold V at reset and discard incoming jumps; a neuron is eligible at t_last+2 ms. At most one spike per neuron per step. Record event times at endpoints. Units remain physical in the model; dimensionless arrays are allowed at connectivity, random-count, observation, serialization and host-analysis boundaries.

## Inspected data contract
- Sources: task text only; workspace initially empty. No measured recordings or literature. Parameters are supplied modeling assumptions, and expected labels are hypotheses.
- Raw results: per run, all-neuron binary spikes on the 0.1-ms grid (losslessly packed if useful), per-bin E/I spike counts, final voltage, graph identity, configuration, code hash, environment/device identity, seeds and execution logs. Preserve all unfavorable runs too.
- Derived: post-burn E/I/all rates in Hz/neuron; individual ISI CV=population-standard-deviation(ISI)/mean(ISI), requiring at least 20 complete post-burn ISIs per neuron; report eligibility fraction and E/I medians/distributions. No CV inference from the raster subset.
- Spectrum: global population rate in 0.1-ms bins, mean removed; Welch density with 1000-ms Hann segments, 50% overlap. Dominant frequency is the maximum PSD bin in [1,500] Hz, reported even if no oscillation is supported. Also preserve raw full-window Fourier density. For peak concentration use total Welch power in [1,500] Hz and power within +/-2 Hz of the dominant bin. Peak-to-background is peak PSD divided by median PSD in [1,500] Hz, excluding +/-5 Hz around that peak.
- Rate/raster mapping: same exact physical window and neuron identities across conditions. Global dashed mean is the mean over the displayed window; full analysis means reported separately.

## Acceptance boundary
- Frozen synchrony statistic: bin global counts in 5 ms. Compute S=sqrt(max(Var(K)-Mean(K),0))/Mean(K), using population variance. This removes the Poisson counting floor and measures macroscopic fractional rate modulation. Synchrony supported if S>=0.10; asynchrony supported if S<=0.05; between these is inconclusive. The two cutoffs distinguish substantial (10%) from small (5%) modulation rather than claiming an exact phase boundary. Half-window S must fall in the same category as full-window S, otherwise stationarity is inconclusive.
- Regular supported if the median individual ISI CV<=0.50; irregular supported if median CV>=0.70. Require at least 50% of neurons eligible for either conclusion. Intermediate CV or insufficient eligibility is inconclusive. Report E/I CV too.
- Oscillation supported if peak/background>=5 AND peak concentration>=0.10. Fast SI requires synchrony, irregularity, oscillation, and dominant frequency>=50 Hz; slow SI requires those same predicates with dominant frequency<50 Hz. The 50-Hz division corresponds to one membrane time constant (1/tau_m), derived from supplied dynamics. SR requires synchrony and regularity; AI requires asynchrony and irregularity. Every condition must satisfy its requested predicates independently for all three seeds to support the requested regime. Mixed-seed evidence is inconclusive; consistent contradictory categorical evidence is unsupported. Do not force labels or retune tests.
- Stationarity: compare E/I rates in the first and second 1.5 s of analysis; if either differs by >20% of the full-window rate, flag transient/nonstationary evidence and withhold regime support. Explicitly report finite-duration and finite-network limits.
- Component checks before production: exponential leak; threshold/reset; exact refractory release; recurrent delay impulse; voltage sign and jump size; Poisson multiple events, sample mean/variance and cross-target independence; full graph fixed indegree/no-autapse/no-duplicate/sign contract; deterministic repeat; compare sparse event propagation with a small explicit sum. Accelerated compiled result must match the component/reference path.
- Numerical control fixed now: rerun all four conditions at dt=0.05 ms for seed 101, with the same physical durations, graph and initial state. Aggregate to 0.1 ms for outputs. Treat control as numerical sensitivity, not an extra evaluation seed. Same distribution of independent Poisson drive, not identical paths. Flag a material discrepancy if E or I mean rate changes by >10% OR supported regularity/synchrony/oscillation category changes OR dominant frequency shifts by >max(5 Hz,10%) when both spectra support oscillations. A flagged discrepancy makes that condition's grid-independent regime claim inconclusive; preserve baseline results and explain it.
- Invalid results: changed supplied parameters, broken unit/event/delay/graph contract, missing raw evidence, nonfinite states, neuron rate above refractory bound (500 Hz apart from finite-window endpoint tolerance), lost output, or unreviewed change to frozen decisions. Timing noise/finite grid concerns are limitations rather than permission to alter inputs.
- Allowed conclusions: descriptive evidence at these four points, this graph ensemble and these durations; unsupported/inconclusive requested labels are acceptable outcomes. No inferred biological realism, reproduction claim, literature agreement, parameter-region claim or forced causal interpretation.
- Literature gate: skipped by explicit researcher restriction; scientific hypotheses will be tested, not imported. Optional training/fitting coverage: none.

name: brainx-acceleration
description: Audits and refactors BrainX/BrainState simulation code for performance using state-aware BrainState transform patterns. Use for speed, acceleration, GPU performance, batching, vectorization, parameter sweeps, many neurons/trials, compile/runtime separation, memory reduction, throughput, multi-device execution, or performance-audit requests.
---

# BrainX acceleration

## Purpose and boundary

Audit or refactor BrainX simulation and training hot paths. Open `brainstate` → `SKILL.md` before a nontrivial State-aware rewrite. Keep the modeling package's orchestrator when it already expresses the scientific operation and the needed execution boundary.

## Underlying mental model

Represent populations and independent trials as array or State axes. Let BrainState control repeated execution so a compiled function can preserve mutation, randomness, and gradients. Prioritize correctness, State and RNG safety, shape stability, warm runtime, memory, then device scale.

## Diagnose and rewrite

1. Inventory the hot call sites. Record loop axes and trip counts, inputs and outputs, State reads and writes, RNG policy, transform boundaries, host transfers, and connectivity representation.
2. Rank by measured impact, semantic risk, and confidence. Identify a small deterministic baseline before changing execution. Open `references/audit-and-rewrite-patterns.md` for search patterns, bottleneck classification, transform compositions, and an audit report template.
3. Rewrite one axis or compilation boundary at a time. Keep units, update order, sparse or event connectivity, and stable shapes, dtypes, and PyTrees. Use BrainState transforms for State effects. Use raw JAX transforms for pure array functions with explicit inputs and outputs. Keep host preprocessing and I/O outside transforms.
4. Map only independent lanes. Declare which State is shared read-only, mapped, written back, or discarded. Split or advance random streams deliberately across lanes and time.
5. Compile the largest stable unit that owns the repeated work. Keep transform construction outside hot loops and benchmark already-fused or I/O-bound work before rewriting it.

| Bottleneck | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Python loop over neurons, features, or compartments | Population-shaped State and array or event operations. |
| Python time loop | `brainstate.transform.for_loop` for input-to-output steps, or `scan` when the body carries an explicit value. Keep only required history. |
| Independent trials or parameter sweeps | Native batching when provided by the model, or a State-aware mapped rollout with explicit State and RNG axes. |
| Parameter perturbation loops | State-aware `grad` for a differentiable objective. Keep per-example gradients for tasks that need them. |
| Long differentiable rollout | Checkpoint the rollout when activation storage dominates. |
| Multi-device workload | Establish an efficient single-device baseline before using `pmap2`, `shard_map`, or explicit sharding. |

## Validate and benchmark

Compare baseline and rewritten outputs, final State, units, and shapes on the same small input with stated tolerances. Check mapped State isolation, repeatable seeds, independent random draws, and gradient or optimizer updates where applicable. Confirm sparse connectivity and required outputs remain intact. Separate compile time from synchronized warm timing, and inspect memory and host transfers.

For an audit, report the bottleneck evidence, affected axis, impact, risk, proposed rewrite, and validation. For a requested rewrite, apply the smallest patch and report actual parity and timing. Keep a measured baseline when the rewrite would change scientific behavior or increase resource use without a measured benefit.

## Reference routing

| Reference | Open when |
|---|---|
| `references/audit-and-rewrite-patterns.md` | Classifying a suspected hot path, selecting among axis compositions, or drafting an acceleration audit. |
| `brainstate` → `references/brainstate/transformation-jit-expansion.md` | Choosing compilation boundaries, static arguments, timing, or diagnosing recompiles. |
| `brainstate` → `references/brainstate/transformation-vmap-expansion.md` | Mapping independent trial, ensemble, State, or RNG axes. |
| `brainstate` → `references/brainstate/transformation-grad-expansion.md` | Differentiating parameters or explicit inputs, or replacing finite differences. |
| `brainstate` → `references/brainstate/brainstate-control-flow-patterns.md` | Selecting a transformed time loop, branch, or checkpointing pattern. |
| `brainstate` → `references/brainstate/randomness-and-reproducibility.md` | Controlling stream independence, restoration, or reproducible replay. |

## Boundaries and common failures

Resolve State and RNG ownership before changing transforms. Keep a known-correct non-transformed path for tiny workloads, irreducibly dynamic shapes, or code dominated by I/O and logging when a transform offers little benefit. Address representation and memory bandwidth before batching a workload that would densify or materialize an unnecessary full history.

- Next action: completed

This is a first-principles experiment derived only from the supplied data. No papers, scientific example scripts, existing model implementations or remembered protocols were consulted. Installed skills and public API contracts were used only for package mechanics. The researcher explicitly delegated every unspecified choice, and [NeuroSpecification.md](NeuroSpecification.md) was locked before implementation or simulation. No scientific parameters, thresholds, seeds, durations or plotted cases were tuned after observing results.

Entries are means across three independent graph/input seeds, with the full min–max range in parentheses; these are descriptive ranges, not confidence intervals. Each CV entry first takes the median over eligible neurons within its run. A spectral maximum is always reported; it establishes an oscillation only when the frozen concentration and background tests also pass.

Each upper panel shows instantaneous global rate in unsmoothed 0.1-ms bins, in Hz per neuron, with its displayed-window mean dashed. Rate axes have independent numeric scales to keep low-rate conditions visible. Each lower panel shows the same randomly selected 50 neurons in the same order. All panels use seed 101 and 3500<t≤4000 ms; no spikes were jittered. The raster supports a visual comparison while the quantitative decisions use the entire post-burn 3 s and all neurons.

E/I rates are post-burn means in Hz per neuron. Each connected pair is one matched graph/input seed; the dashed black pair is the seed101 fine-grid control.
